name: Mexican Chorizo and Egg Casserole
writer_notes: SOURCE YIELD 10, rebuilt to 14 at the mapper's 1.4x scale. Every gram and buy string transcribed from mapped\mexican-chorizo-egg-casserole.json; no number computed in prose.

Our honest fresh-Mexican-chorizo build lands 532 / 27 / 17 / 39. The mapper pins the entire gap on the source's nutrition plugin booking DRY SPANISH chorizo (455 cal / 24.1 P / 38.3 F per 100 g) for the string 'chorizo sausage', while the dish as written - skillet-browned, a Mexican breakfast/dinner casserole - uses FRESH Mexican chorizo (the Cacique label row, 190 cal / 9 P / 16 F per 70 g raw), which is the product the board prices. The main protein is WEIGHT-anchored (1 lb printed, our only drift is -1.8% quantization to 22 oz), so no each-weight assumption exists to be wrong. Rebuilding our exact line set on the dry-Spanish basis reproduces the source's figures within 6% on all four macros. Protein cross-check gap is -17.9% (outside the 15% instrument) and is kept, not fixed, because the identical-basis reconstruction explains it. If QA disagrees, the line to re-examine is the chorizo row, not the portion. Southwest documented-divergence precedent.

BUTTER NOT BOOKED (source defect, transcribed as printed): the source lists butter for greasing the 9x13 dish only in its instructions, never in its ingredient list. The mapper did not book it (a greasing film is sub-10-cal per serving and the printed list governs). The make_it steps therefore say 'grease' / 'nonstick spray or a little oil' and never name butter, keeping greasing a pantry-static gimme, not a shopping line - the jalapeno-popper-chicken-casserole precedent. No make_it step names an ingredient that is not on the buy list.

OPTIONAL TOPPINGS NOT COSTED, NOT STEPPED: the source's final line suggests serving with pico de gallo, sour cream, and avocado or guacamole. These are unquantified optional garnishes with no gram basis; the mapper excluded them from band macros and pico de gallo has no commodity (enqueued OPTIONAL). They appear ONLY as an optional 'if you like' aside in the intro, never as a numbered make_it step and never on the buy list, so no step touches an unbought ingredient and the per-serving numbers do not silently absorb an uncosted line.

EVERY BOUGHT INGREDIENT IS USED BY A STEP and no step uses anything unbought. Walked both directions: chorizo, yellow onion, red bell pepper, garlic (make_it 3 - the browned base); pepper jack, cheddar, cilantro, green onions, jalapeno (make_it 4 - the cheese mix); corn tortillas (make_it 5 - the layers); eggs, half and half, hot sauce, black pepper (make_it 6 - the custard). All 14 costed lines are used; the only thing a step names that is not a costed line is greasing the dish, treated pantry-static.

SHOP_SMART makes NO per-ounce, leftover, or lasts-several-batches claim, so no bullet needs a cost_lines entry to prove it. Every statement is grounded in the recipe's own buy amount or in product-type / cooking guidance (fresh vs dry chorizo, corn vs flour tortillas, half-and-half vs milk set). GRAMS are the mapper's: chorizo 624 (1 lb 6 oz, weight-anchored), onion 113, red bell 90, garlic 21, pepper jack 319, cheddar 319 (both weight-anchored at 11 1/4 oz), green onions 90, cilantro 5.3, jalapeno 42, eggs 850 (17 large), half and half 1020, hot sauce 3.8, black pepper 1.7, corn tortillas 306 (13). intro_html: Chorizo and eggs is a breakfast a lot of us grew up on, and this casserole takes that same skillet and stretches it into a week of dinners. Fresh Mexican chorizo browns down with onion, sweet red pepper, and garlic. That gets layered between quartered corn tortillas and a double hit of pepper jack and sharp cheddar, then the whole pan is flooded with an egg and half and half custard shot through with jalapeno, green onion, and cilantro. It rests overnight so the tortillas drink up the custard, then bakes into something you can cut into fourteen honest squares. Built at 14 servings it runs about {{cal}} calories and {{protein}} grams of protein a serving, with about 17 grams of carbs. That is a low-carb dinner that eats like a lazy weekend breakfast. Dress a square with a spoon of pico, sour cream, or avocado if you like, though the numbers above are the casserole on its own.

cost_closing_html: About ${{cost_ps}} a serving (at everyday cost) for a baked chorizo and egg casserole that cuts into fourteen square, protein-heavy dinners. The chorizo, cheese, and eggs carry it; the peppers, onion, and herbs do the bright work, and the whole thing costs less than the drive-through breakfast it out-eats.
shop_smart: Buy FRESH Mexican chorizo, not the dry cured kind. You want about a pound and a half of the soft, uncooked chorizo that lives in tubes in the refrigerated case, the stuff that browns like loose sausage. The hard, dry-cured Spanish sausage on the shelf is a different animal and will not melt into the base the way this dish needs. This is the flavor of the whole casserole and a real share of the protein.

Two cheeses, about eleven ounces of each. Pepper jack brings the gentle heat and cheddar brings the sharp, and you need roughly the same amount of each, shredded. Buy blocks and shred them yourself, or grab the pre-shredded bags if you would rather trade a little money for time. Either way this is a low-carb, calorie-honest dinner, so reach for the full-fat cheese the numbers are built on.

Seventeen eggs and about a quart of half and half are the custard. This is what sets the whole pan, so do not swap the half and half for milk, which sets thinner and looser. Whisk them together with the hot sauce and black pepper until it is a little bubbly, and let the raw pan rest overnight so the tortillas soften into the egg instead of staying dry.

Thirteen corn tortillas are the structure and nearly all the carbs. Quarter them and they become the layers that hold everything together. Keep them corn, not flour, both for the flavor that makes this taste Mexican and because flour would push the carb count up. This is where most of the 17 grams a serving comes from.

The fresh crew does the loud work for pennies. Onion, red bell pepper, garlic, a bundle of green onions, a handful of cilantro, and a few jalapenos are cheap produce that carry most of the flavor. Seed and devein the jalapenos so you get steady warmth instead of a surprise, and slice the green onions and chop the cilantro fresh so they stay bright in the finished bake.
make_it: Weigh your empty baking dish and write the number down. You will need it at the end to split this into 14 even servings by weight, which is the only honest way to portion one big casserole.

In a large skillet, brown the fresh chorizo with the chopped onion, red bell pepper, and garlic over medium heat until the chorizo is cooked through and the vegetables are soft. Pull it off the heat and set it aside.
In a medium bowl, toss the shredded pepper jack and cheddar together with the cilantro, sliced green onions, and chopped jalapenos until the cheese is evenly flecked with green. Set it aside.
Grease a large, deep baking dish, or split the recipe across two dishes if yours is a standard 9 by 13, since 14 servings is a lot of casserole. Nonstick spray or a light film of oil is all you need.

Spread a third of the quartered tortillas across the bottom, then a third of the chorizo mixture, then a third of the cheese mixture. Repeat the layers twice more, finishing with a cheese layer on top.

In a large bowl, whisk the eggs with the half and half, hot sauce, and black pepper until fully combined and a little bubbly. Pour it evenly over the layered dish so it soaks down through the tortillas.
Cover and refrigerate at least 6 hours or overnight so the tortillas drink up the custard. This rest is not optional; it is what turns loose layers into a sliceable casserole.

Bake at 350 degrees F for 60 to 90 minutes, until the top is golden and a fork slid into the center comes out clean, like testing a cake. Let it rest 10 minutes, then weigh the dish, subtract the empty weight from Step 1, and divide across 14 containers.
portion_html: Set the baked dish on your scale and subtract the empty weight you wrote down in Step 1 to get the total. Divide that number by 14 and scoop that exact weight into each container. Every serving lands near {{cal}} calories with {{protein}} grams of protein.
